item.title: Air pollution Mitigation in Petroleum refineries
item.description:
Refineries are one of the biggest industries in the world since we are surviving in a hydrocarbon economy. Petroleum is the raw material for a lot of industries such as pharmaceuticals, polymers, fertillizers, pesticides etc. It unites the anthropogenic activities around the world and processes around 3.5 billion ton of crude and around 2.5 giga of natural gas every year. Hence it becomes important to mitigate and control the pollutants that are released by a refinery as flue. Major air pollutants in a petroleum refinery include

Carbon dioxide (about 10 million metric tonnes)
Volatile Organic Compounds
Carbon Monoxide
Hydrogen Sulphide
Sulphur Oxides
Nitrogen Oxides
Particulate Matters
Most of these air pollutants are combustion emissions.


Mitigation Strategies

Technological Control Measures

Desulfurization Units:
Use hydrodesulfurization to remove sulfur compounds from crude oil by reacting them with hydrogen at high temperatures and pressures.
Flue Gas Scrubbers:
Employ wet or dry scrubbers to remove SO₂ from flue gases using alkaline substances like lime (CaO) or limestone (CaCO₃).
Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR):
Reduce NOₓ by injecting ammonia (NH₃) into flue gases over a catalyst.
Electrostatic Precipitators (ESP):
Remove particulate matter by charging particles and collecting them on oppositely charged plates.
Vapor Recovery Units (VRUs):
Capture VOCs from storage tanks and transport systems for reuse.

Process Optimization

Low-NOx Burners:
Optimize combustion conditions to minimize NOₓ formation by controlling flame temperature and excess oxygen levels.
Energy Recovery:
Recover waste heat from flue gases using heat exchangers to improve energy efficiency and reduce fuel consumption.

Fugitive Emission Control

Leak Detection and Repair (LDAR):
Employ infrared cameras and gas analyzers to identify and repair leaks from valves, seals, and flanges.
Double-Seal Storage Tanks:
Use advanced sealing technologies to prevent VOC emissions from storage tanks.

Green Alternatives and Carbon Capture

Green Fuels:
Transition to biofuels or hydrogen as a cleaner alternative to conventional hydrocarbons.
Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS):
Capture CO₂ emissions and store them underground in geological formations to prevent release into the atmosphere.

Regulatory Compliance and Monitoring

Continuous Emission Monitoring Systems (CEMS):
Install systems to monitor emissions of SO₂, NOₓ, CO₂, and VOCs in real time.
Adherence to Standards:
Follow international guidelines, such as the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) regulations or the European Union Industrial Emissions Directive.
Community and Environmental Protection

Green Buffers:
Plant vegetation around refinery sites to act as natural barriers against air pollutants.
Public Health Monitoring:
Conduct regular health assessments in nearby communities to address pollution-related illnesses.
By combining advanced technologies, process optimization, and regulatory compliance, refineries can significantly reduce their emissions and mitigate environmental and health impacts.

Conclusion
Since petroleum refineries are one of the largest industrial sector in this world, it is important to mitigate the pollutants of this industry to avoid a rise in anthropogenic pollutants. It is important for different stakeholders (citizines, companies and governments) to mitigate air pollution caused by the petroleum refinery and have stringent measures in place. Environment friendly and green technologies can help in the longer run along with raising awareness amongst the people.

References

Sofia, D., Gioiella, F., Lotrecchiano, N. et al. Mitigation strategies for reducing air pollution. Environ Sci Pollut Res 27, 19226–19235 (2020). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11356-020-08647-x

item.description:
The Husky Superior Refinery incident occurred on April 26, 2018, in Superior, Wisconsin, during a planned maintenance shutdown of the Fluid Catalytic Cracking (FCC) unit. An explosion in the FCC unit propelled debris that punctured a nearby asphalt storage tank, leading to the release of approximately 17,000 barrels of hot asphalt, which subsequently ignited and caused multiple fires. This series of events resulted in injuries to 36 workers and necessitated the evacuation of over 2,500 residents from the City of Superior.
The U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board (CSB) conducted an investigation into the incident and released its final report on December 29, 2022. The report identified several key safety issues, including:
Transient Operation Safeguards: The importance of separating air from flammable hydrocarbons during FCC unit shutdowns to prevent explosive mixtures. At the time of the incident, essential safeguards were either not implemented or ineffective.
Process Knowledge: Employees lacked adequate understanding of the FCC unit's transient operation hazards, partly due to limited engagement with external experts and other refineries.
Process Safety Management: Deficiencies were found in maintaining process safety information, operating procedures, process hazard analyses, and operator training related to the FCC unit.
Industry Knowledge and Guidance: Despite previous similar incidents, such as the 2015 explosion at an FCC unit in California, lessons were not effectively learned or applied at the Superior Refinery.
Brittle Fracture During Extreme Events: The vessels involved failed by brittle fracture, sending metal debris throughout the refinery. The materials used were not of newer grades of steel recommended for better toughness properties.
Emergency Preparedness: The refinery was unable to prevent the asphalt from catching fire due to the size of the release and competing priorities during the emergency response.
The CSB issued 16 safety recommendations to various entities, including the company, the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and the American Petroleum Institute (API). Notably, the CSB called on the EPA to develop a program prioritizing inspections of FCC units in refineries that operate hydrofluoric acid alkylation units, to verify safeguards that prevent explosions during transient operations.
For a visual representation and further insights, the CSB released a safety video on June 9, 2023, detailing the events leading up to the incident and the investigation findings.
This incident underscores the critical importance of robust safety measures, thorough employee training, and effective emergency preparedness in preventing and mitigating industrial accidents, particularly during non-routine operations such as shutdowns and startups.
Here’s a detailed expansion of the Husky Superior Refinery incident based on the points you provided:

When and Where
The accident occurred on April 26, 2018, at the Husky Superior Refinery in Superior, Wisconsin, during a planned shutdown for maintenance. The explosion originated in the Fluid Catalytic Cracking (FCC) unit, a key component of the refinery's operations. The blast caused extensive damage, injured 36 workers, and led to the evacuation of over 2,500 residents due to the release and ignition of hazardous materials.


Chemistry
The incident stemmed from the handling of hydrocarbons and air during the FCC unit's shutdown. When hydrocarbons and oxygen mix in the presence of a heat source, they can form an explosive environment. In this case:
The FCC unit contained combustible hydrocarbons mixed with oxygen, which should have been purged during the shutdown.
The ignition source for the explosion was likely residual heat or sparks from nearby equipment.
The explosion ruptured a storage tank containing approximately 17,000 barrels of asphalt, which is a high-viscosity hydrocarbon. When exposed to the heat of the explosion, the asphalt ignited, leading to extensive fires.


Prevention
The U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board (CSB) highlighted several preventive measures to avoid such incidents:
Transient Operation Safeguards: Ensure hydrocarbons and oxygen are separated during shutdowns to prevent explosive conditions.
Process Safety Training: Provide workers with better knowledge of transient operation risks.
Industry Knowledge Sharing: Learn from similar past incidents in other refineries to implement best practices.
Modern Materials: Use newer grades of steel for vessels to resist brittle fractures during extreme conditions.
Regular Safety Audits: Strengthen compliance with safety standards through frequent inspections.


Reasons for Puncture
The explosion in the FCC unit sent metal debris flying, which punctured the nearby asphalt storage tank. Key reasons for the puncture included:
Brittle Fracture of Metal: The FCC unit and other equipment were made of older grades of steel, which failed under high stress.
High-Pressure Shockwaves: The force of the explosion created strong shockwaves, compromising the structural integrity of nearby equipment.
Inadequate Separation: The tank was located too close to the FCC unit, making it vulnerable to damage.


Measures Taken
Following the incident, several measures were implemented to improve safety and prevent similar accidents:
Improved Inspection Programs: The CSB recommended prioritizing inspections of FCC units and ensuring compliance with modern safety protocols.
Enhanced Emergency Preparedness: Husky Energy and local authorities strengthened their emergency response plans to handle such incidents better.
Upgraded Materials: Refineries were encouraged to replace older steel equipment with materials more resistant to brittle fractures.
Process Safety Management Improvements: OSHA and the EPA were urged to enhance regulatory oversight of transient operations and FCC unit safety.
Training and Awareness: Increased focus on training refinery workers to recognize and mitigate transient operation hazards.
These measures aim to enhance refinery safety standards and prevent future incidents during high-risk operations like shutdowns and startups.
